newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - Low prices hammer Highveld Steel.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Low prices hammer Highveld Steel.

text.p: Low steel and ferro-alloy prices on international markets last year will deal a major blow to year earnings at South African steel producer Highveld Steel and Vanadium Corp Ltd, analysts said.
They forcast earnings of between 73 and 85 cents per share, down from 218.6 in 1995, when the company reports its results for the year to December 31, 1996, on Monday.
"I am looking at a substantial drop in earnings for 1996. The results that you are going to see are fairly disastrous," Troye Brady of Societe Generale Frankel Pollak told Reuters.
He said Highveld Steel had suffered huge losses from its stainless joint-venture, Columbus Stainless, which has been riddled with commissioning problems in the last year.
Columbus -- one of the world's biggest stainless steel prouducers -- is a joint-venture between Highveld Steel, Samancor Ltd and the state's Industrial Development Corporation.
One analyst who did not want to be named put loses from Columbus at around 50 million rand in 1996 for Highveld Steel.
"It's not only that (commissioning problems), it's also that they are not getting a very good price for their stainless steel," George Grohmann of stockbroker Rice Rinaldi said.
He said new capacity and overproduction had sent steel prices plummeting in 1996.
"Stainless steel is very much overproduced at the moment...In 1995 and 1996 we got a lot of extra production coming on stream, new capacity and expansions," Grohmann added.
Analysts polled by Reuters forecast a dividend of between 32 and 40 cents, with a consensus at 35.6 cents, down from 90 cents in 1995.
A strike late last year is also expected to take its toll.
About 2,000 workers had downed tools in October last year at Highveld Steel's iron and steelworks operations after a black artisan had allegedly been assaulted by a white supervisor.
However, analysts expected Highveld Steel to pick up performance during the course of 1997, saying a relatively weaker rand could help earnings in the first half.
Improving vanadium and steel prices should also help.
